editorial.headline: Residential Care Intermediation: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers paid matchmaking between clients and residential-care providers, online or offline; it is fully open to foreign investment nationally and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Residential-care intermediation is the business of bringing together people seeking residential-care services and the providers able to deliver them. The intermediary is paid a fee or commission, which may come from either the client or the provider. It is a matching and access function, rather than the provision of care itself: the business can earn from commissions and may also draw revenue from sources such as advertising.

The activity is deliberately channel-neutral. It can be operated through a digital platform, but it does not depend on one. Face-to-face introductions, door-to-door activity, telephone and correspondence all fall within the stated scope. That makes this a practical category for businesses whose value lies in organising demand, presenting providers, and facilitating the connection between the two. Intermediation involving medical, dental and other human-health services is outside this activity’s scope.

The registration picture is broad. The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale, and its scope expressly addresses non-exempt electronic-trading organisers and intermediary-facility organisers, whether established within Indonesia’s legal territory or established abroad while conducting electronic-trading activity in Indonesia. It also extends beyond those organisers to other businesses undertaking the activity. Nationally, foreign investment is TERBUKA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In plain terms, the record sets no foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity at the national level.

Bali does not reverse that national opening. Its status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record explains that, at Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. As a result, the activity is not blocked by the island-wide, permanent Bali moratorium that applies to PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. A foreign investor can therefore approach registration in Bali on the same essential premise as nationally: the activity is open, with full foreign ownership permitted, and it is not caught by that moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: For this activity, Bali does not reverse the national position: full foreign ownership is permitted and the PMA moratorium does not block registration.
